reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A true osteonecrosis affecting the lunate, the central carpal bone of the proximal row, rather than a traction apophysitis
Typically presents in young adults, often manual labourers aged roughly twenty to forty, and is uncommon in children
Complaints include activity-related dorsal wrist pain, stiffness, swelling, reduced grip strength and limited wrist extension
The radiographic hallmark is early sclerosis (increased density) of the lunate, progressing to fragmentation, collapse and eventual carpal disruption
Frequently associated with a negative ulnar variance (relatively short ulna), which is thought to concentrate load across the lunate
The Lichtman staging system, based on lunate density, collapse and carpal alignment, guides treatment selection
Early disease may be radiographically silent, so magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for confirming devascularisation and marrow change
Management ranges from immobilisation and activity modification in early stages to joint-levelling, revascularisation or salvage surgery as needed for advanced collapse
reference.pathophysiology: Kienbock disease is an osteonecrosis of the lunate in which the bone loses its blood supply and undergoes progressive death, collapse and fragmentation. The cause is regarded as multifactorial, combining interruption of the tenuous intraosseous and extraosseous vascular supply with mechanical overload. A relatively short ulna (negative ulnar variance) is commonly present and is believed to increase compressive stress on the lunate, while repetitive loading and single or repeated microtrauma may precipitate ischaemia. As the necrotic bone weakens it fractures and collapses, altering carpal mechanics, producing proximal migration of the capitate and rotation of the scaphoid, and ultimately leading to secondary degenerative arthritis of the wrist.
additionalDifferentials: Scapholunate ligament injury and carpal instability
De Quervain tenosynovitis or other wrist tendinopathy
Ganglion cyst causing dorsal wrist pain
additionalInvestigations: Plain wrist radiographs including a neutral posteroanterior view to assess ulnar variance and lunate density
Magnetic resonance imaging to detect early avascular change before collapse is visible on plain films
Computed tomography to define fragmentation, collapse and articular surface integrity
Comparison of ulnar variance with the contralateral wrist
Bone scintigraphy where diagnostic uncertainty remains and cross-sectional imaging is unavailable
Staging assessment using the Lichtman classification to plan treatment
redFlags: Progressive lunate collapse with carpal shortening indicating advanced, potentially irreversible disease
Established secondary wrist arthritis with persistent pain and functional loss
Fixed loss of grip and wrist motion suggesting carpal disintegration
Bilateral or atypical presentation prompting consideration of an underlying systemic cause of osteonecrosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the stage at presentation; early disease treated with offloading or joint-levelling procedures may preserve function, whereas advanced lunate collapse and carpal disruption tend to progress to degenerative wrist arthritis with lasting stiffness and reduced grip.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent wrist pain to a soft-tissue strain and missing early sclerosis on plain films
Relying on normal early radiographs and failing to obtain magnetic resonance imaging when suspicion is high
Overlooking negative ulnar variance as a contributing mechanical factor
Underestimating carpal collapse and applying joint-preserving surgery when salvage is more appropriate
